candidates.statement: Regenerative medicine therapies intended to treat, modify, reverse, or cure serious conditions are 90 eligible for FDA’s expedited programs, including fast track designation, breakthrough therapy 91 designation, RMAT designation, accelerated approval, and priority review designation, if they 92 meet the criteria for such programs. This guidance provides additional information about the 93 application of those programs to regenerative medicine therapies, as well as information about 94 the RMAT designation program, which CBER intends to administer in a manner that is 95 consistent with the other expedited programs, where applicable. Sponsors should consult the 96 “Guidance for Industry: Expedited Programs for Serious Conditions – Drugs and Biologics” 97 dated May 2014 (Expedited Programs Guidance) (Ref. 2) for generally applicable information, 98 including the criteria for, and benefits of, fast track designation, breakthrough therapy 99 designation, accelerated approval, and priority review designation. 11 As with other biological 100 products, regenerative medicine therapies receiving fast track designation, breakthrough therapy 101 designation, and RMAT designation must meet the evidentiary standards for approval, including 102 demonstrating safety and effectiveness (regardless of whether the product receives accelerated or 103 traditional approval). 12
candidates.context: In 1988, FDA issued regulations in 21 CFR Part 312 (Subpart E) 10 on expediting the availability 80 of promising therapies to patients with serious conditions. The regulations call for earlier 81 attention to drugs that have promise in treating such conditions, including early consultation with 82 FDA for sponsors of such products. In subsequent years, the FD&C Act has been amended 83 several times to include several new programs for expedited product development and review, 84 including fast track designation, accelerated approval, and breakthrough therapy designation. In 85 December 2016, Congress amended section 506 of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 356) by adding 86 new section 506(g), which specifically addresses the expedited development and review of 87 certain regenerative medicine therapies designated as RMATs. 88 9 For additional information, see 21 USC 353(g)(1)(C) and 21 CFR 3.2.

candidates.statement: It should be noted that the level of evidence required for breakthrough therapy 211 designation is higher than for fast track designation. Specifically, fast track designation 212 requires only that nonclinical or clinical data demonstrate the potential to address an 213 unmet medical need, whereas for breakthrough therapy designation, preliminary clinical 214 evidence must indicate that the product may demonstrate a substantial improvement over 215 existing therapies on one or more clinically significant endpoints. 216
candidates.context: Under the breakthrough therapy program, an investigational new drug that is intended to 202 treat a serious condition, and for which preliminary clinical evidence indicates that the 203 product may demonstrate substantial improvement over available therapies on one or 204 more clinically significant endpoints, may qualify for breakthrough therapy designation. 205 Advantages of this designation incorporate all the benefits of fast track designation and 206 also include intensive FDA guidance on efficient drug development, as well as an 207 organizational commitment to involve senior management in facilitating the product’s 208 development program. 209 The following are hypothetical examples of regenerative medicine therapies that CBER 218 may consider for breakthrough therapy designation: 219

candidates.statement: Regarding the preliminary clinical evidence to demonstrate the potential of a regenerative 259 medicine therapy to address unmet medical needs, we generally expect that such 260 evidence would be obtained from clinical investigations specifically conducted to assess 261 the effects of the therapy on a serious condition. Such clinical investigations may not 262 always be prospective clinical trials with a concurrent control. In some cases, clinical 263 evidence obtained from relevant clinical investigations with appropriately chosen 264 external controls 16 may provide sufficient preliminary clinical evidence of the potential to 265 address an unmet medical need. In other cases, preliminary clinical evidence could come 266 from well-designed retrospective studies or clinical case series that provide data 267 systematically collected by treating physicians. Such clinical evidence may be from 268 studies conducted outside of the United States 17 (Ref. 4). While preliminary clinical 269 evidence does not need to demonstrate the substantial evidence of effectiveness that 270 would be necessary for approval, such information should not be purely hypothetical and 271 should show the potential to address an unmet medical need. candidates.statement: Due to their distinctive features, regenerative medicine therapies are likely to raise unique safety 587 considerations that would benefit from long-term safety monitoring. Many regenerative 588 medicine therapies are intended to be administered once and designed to achieve prolonged 589 biological activity. Since the biological activity of many regenerative medicine therapies may 590 develop or manifest differently when compared to conventional pharmaceuticals (e.g., small 591 molecules), monitoring plans for clinical studies should include assessments for both safety and 592 any pharmacologic activity that presents product-specific safety concerns. We recommend that 593 sponsors include in their specific monitoring plans both short-term and long-term safety 594 monitoring, where the duration of long-term safety monitoring should be based on the type of the 595 regenerative medicine therapy product. 30 Sponsors are encouraged to explore the feasibility of 596 leveraging digital health technologies for collecting the safety information necessary for 597 achieving the goals of monitoring and follow up. 31
candidates.context: • For regenerative medicine therapies that are cellular or tissue constructs intended to 581 replace a tissue or organ, CBER recognizes that assessment of the long-term 582 effectiveness of the construct might not be feasible prior to marketing approval. For 583 these products, CBER could consider short-term performance to be novel, clinically 584 meaningful efficacy endpoints. 585 We encourage sponsors of regenerative medicine therapies to have early discussions with CBER 600 about clinical trial design (Ref. 8), including the appropriate study population and the number of 601 study subjects that might be necessary to provide sufficient evidence of safety and effectiveness. 602
